newsitem.title: POLAND: EU entry talks might start in April - Poland.
newsitem.headline: EU entry talks might start in April - Poland.

text.p: Poland is getting signals from Brussels that the EU's accession talks with new members may start in April or May next year rather than January as was planned, Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati said on Tuesday.
Rosati said Poland counted on starting talks as agreed in January, six months after the EU's inter-governmental conference, due to end with the current summit in Amsterdam.
"But signals are flowing from Brussels 'Oh don't be so sure that it will be exactly January, it could be April'," he told a meeting of the Business Centre Club employers' group in Warsaw.

"We are disappointed that the European Union is not able to clearly state the start of these talks and to finish the conference in accordance with plan. But whether it is January or April, there is no point in entering a collective dispute with the EU," Rosati said.

He put the chances of the talks starting in April or May rather than January at 75 percent to 25 percent and said that while Poland was not particularly uneasy, it would have been better politically to start as planned.

Poland expects to be among the first group of former Soviet bloc states to begin the talks, although it has had trade disputes with the EU and expects criticisms when the EU on July 16 delivers its so-called avis opinion on candidates' progress in preparations for entry.
Rosati, stressing that he was speaking before the end of the Amsterdam summit, said it had left some issues unresolved and this could hinder Poland's planning of its approach.
But some questions would be ironed out in coming months and did not arouse great uncertainty in Warsaw.

Rosati saw a bright side in a lack of final decisions at Amsterdam on other weighty matters which he said would be resolved at a summit in a few years' time -- saying that Poland expected to be an EU member by then and therefore have a say.
These concerned, for example, its joint decision making process, the numbers of European Commissioners, and security and foreign policy matters.
"Maybe it is better some mattters won't be foreordained because that means they can be taken with our participation if we manage to join the EU in four or five years," Rosati said.
The Polish minister said Poland was likely to join the EU in around 2001 or 2002, but the exact date was not crucial.
